title: Annotatio III §.XI (7) cont.: Christ and John appeal to sense (Luke 24:39; 1 John 1:1) — many senses surer than one
pass_a_gloss: (3) by appealing to the testimony of the Senses in confirming and establishing the Truth from itself, both through Christ Himself: See my hands and my feet, for I myself am; Handle me and see, for a Spirit has not Flesh and BONES as you see me have (Luke 24:39), and through Christ’s most beloved Apostle: That which was from the beginning &c. (1 John 1:1). But if faith is rightly to be had even in one Sense well constituted and destitute of no requisite for sensing, how much more in several: Since the more species conspiring among themselves are excited in various ways, the more certain is perception, which is their contemplation. Whence by the frequent use of all men, they trust more senses more than one or another.
pass_b_english: (3) Christ and John appeal to sense to confirm truth: Luke 24:39 (handle me; a spirit has not flesh and bones); 1 John 1:1 (that which was from the beginning).
If one well-constituted sense deserves faith, how much more several conspiring species — all men trust many senses more than one.
source_text: (3) Ad Sensuum testimonium, in Veritate à se confirmanda stabiliendaque, provocando, tùm per Christum ipsum: Vide manus meas & pedes meos, nam ego ipse sum, Contrectate me & videte, nam Spiritus Carnem & OSSA non habet, sicut me conspicitis habere Luc. 24. 39. tùm per dilectissimum Christi Apostolum: Quod erat à principio &c. 1. Joh. 1, 1. Quod si verò vel uni Sensui benè constituto, nec requisito ullo ad sentiendum destituto, fides meritò habenda, quantò magis pluribus: Cùm, quò plures species, inter se conspirantes, variis modis excitantur, eò perceptio, quæ est earum contemplatio, certior sit. Unde omnium hominum usu frequentatum, ut pluribus Sensibus magis credant, quàm uni atque alteri.
